passages.title: The Preacher asks what work gains
passages.summary: The Preacher describes generations, wind, and rivers repeating their courses. He asks what lasting gain work brings.
passages.uncertainty: Jerusalem supplies the opening speaker’s setting.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies what gives temporary life lasting value. Why does the Preacher compare human work with wind and rivers?

contextNote.title: Repeated cycles question the promise of lasting gain
contextNote.text: The opening moves through generations, weather, and water. These cycles place human effort within a world that continues beyond each person. The question concerns lasting gain, not whether any work can matter. Read repeated activity beside the speaker’s search for what remains. The book tests the claims people make for achievement.

passages.title: Pleasure and great works do not last
passages.summary: The Preacher builds houses, plants gardens, gathers wealth, and buys servants. He still finds no lasting gain.
passages.uncertainty: Jerusalem supplies the opening speaker’s setting.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies mortal life as temporary. Why does leaving his work to another person trouble the Preacher?

contextNote.title: Inheritance interrupts achievement
contextNote.text: The speaker must leave the results of work to another person. He cannot control that person’s wisdom or use of the inheritance. Achievement therefore includes a future beyond the achiever’s authority.

passages.title: Changing times and shared death
passages.summary: The Preacher lists times for opposite actions. He describes injustice and asks what happens after death.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies wisdom while recognizing life’s limits. Why does the Preacher connect enjoyment of work with what people cannot know?

contextNote.title: A list of times does not grant control
contextNote.text: The paired activities describe many changing conditions of life. Knowing that each has a time does not reveal the whole divine work. The movement from order to limited understanding keeps the poem from promising complete foresight.

passages.title: Power, lonely work, and companions
passages.summary: The Preacher sees people harmed without comfort. He compares a lonely worker with helpful companions.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: What does a companion provide that the lonely worker’s wealth cannot?

contextNote.title: Observation exposes the limits of private advice
contextNote.text: The speaker sees oppression and finds no comfort for its victims. Power remains with those who cause the harm. This observation interrupts any easy account of effort bringing success. Later praise of companionship answers one kind of isolation. It does not claim that friendship alone repairs public injustice.

passages.title: Listen before making promises
passages.summary: The Preacher warns against careless promises to God. He describes wealth that prevents sleep or disappears.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Why does the Preacher prefer making no promise to leaving one unpaid?

contextNote.title: Words before God create obligations
contextNote.text: The warning about vows follows the instruction to listen in worship. An easy promise can produce duties the speaker will not fulfill. The chapter questions impressive speech before turning to the uncertain value of wealth.

passages.title: Having wealth without enjoying it
passages.summary: The Preacher describes a wealthy person unable to enjoy his goods. He asks who knows what is good.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: How does the wealthy person’s experience challenge measuring life by possessions?

contextNote.title: Possession and enjoyment can separate
contextNote.text: The opening describes someone with wealth but no power to enjoy it. Long life and many children do not automatically repair that lack. The argument distinguishes having desirable things from receiving a satisfying life.

passages.title: Mourning and unfair outcomes
passages.summary: The Preacher considers mourning, patience, and unfair outcomes. He also describes a woman as a trap.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Why does the Preacher think a house of mourning can teach the living?

contextNote.title: A funeral teaches what amusement can conceal
contextNote.text: The comparison between mourning and feasting makes mortality a source of instruction. The speaker then offers sayings that resist easy judgments about success. Limits can teach without making every painful event desirable.

passages.title: A ruler’s power and delayed justice
passages.summary: The Preacher advises care before a king. He sees wrongdoers prosper and good people suffer.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: How does delayed punishment affect the people who watch wrongdoing?

contextNote.title: Observed injustice strains a familiar rule
contextNote.text: The speaker sees righteous people receiving what wicked people seem to deserve. His search does not uncover the entire divine work. This admission limits claims that wisdom can explain every outcome.

passages.title: Death, chance, and forgotten wisdom
passages.summary: The Preacher urges enjoyment of food, work, and marriage. He recalls a poor man saving a city.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Why do the poor man’s useful words fail to bring him lasting honor?

contextNote.title: Useful wisdom can remain unrecognized
contextNote.text: A poor wise person rescues a city but receives no lasting remembrance. The example separates wisdom’s value from the honor its possessor gains. The chapter’s attention to death makes that failure of memory more serious.

passages.title: Small mistakes and careless rulers
passages.summary: The Preacher compares foolishness with flies spoiling perfume. He describes poor choices by rulers and workers.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: How does the blunt axe show the value of preparing before work?

contextNote.title: Skill matters within a fragile world
contextNote.text: A blunt tool requires effort that preparation could reduce. The image gives wisdom a practical benefit. Nearby examples of small mistakes still show how easily good work can be damaged.

passages.title: Act without knowing every outcome
passages.summary: The Preacher urges giving, sowing seed, and enjoying youth. He warns that people cannot predict every result.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Scripture Helps connects bread on water with giving without expecting immediate repayment. Why does the Preacher tell the worker to sow in morning and evening?

contextNote.title: Uncertainty can become an excuse for inaction
contextNote.text: Watching wind and clouds can prevent sowing altogether. The speaker recommends work without complete knowledge of its outcome. This response to limits differs from pretending those limits have disappeared.

passages.title: Remember your Creator before old age
passages.summary: The Preacher describes fading strength and death. The closing writer praises his teaching and urges obedience to God.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects lasting value with fearing God and keeping his commands. What does remembering the Creator change before the losses described in this chapter?

contextNote.title: The ending places limits around learning
contextNote.text: The closing warning names the endless production of books. It follows a description of carefully arranged teaching. Learning has value, but accumulation can exhaust the learner. Read the warning beside the final call to responsibility before God. More words do not automatically produce a better life.
